Spatial computing

Spatial UI

Designing Microsoft Teams for Apple Vision Pro required more than adapting screens. It required defining how a mature collaboration product behaves in a spatial environment while preserving clarity, hierarchy, and enterprise trust.

First person case study Editorial layout System driven storytelling
Overview / Context

Defining a spatial model, not isolated screens

As part of Microsoft Teams core design, I led spatial design for the first Teams experience on Apple Vision Pro. Existing patterns could not simply be placed into three dimensional space. They had to be reinterpreted through a new interaction model while preserving familiarity, consistency, and enterprise reliability.

Rather than designing one off views, I focused on a framework that design and engineering could apply across the product. That meant defining hierarchy, depth behavior, window relationships, and accessibility as a coherent system.

What this required

System principles before interface decisions

  • Use depth to communicate hierarchy, not decoration
  • Preserve recognizable Teams behavior across contexts
  • Treat accessibility as a structural input
  • Support flexibility without losing orientation
Chapter

Designing for Spatial Interaction

I structured the work around a set of focused explorations. Each one addressed a core constraint introduced by spatial computing, from authentication and presence to windowing and state management.

System Integration

Secure entry without added friction

Enterprise access in spatial computing still depends on trust, identity, and secure device registration. Core authentication patterns needed to work seamlessly within the new environment without becoming visually heavy.

I integrated Microsoft Authenticator directly into the experience to support sign in and device registration. Registration state, validation, and device status were presented clearly so users could complete setup tasks without unnecessary complexity.

Focused Collaboration

Meetings designed around one primary surface

I designed meetings around a single primary surface. Shared content remains the visual anchor, while participant video and controls stay available as supporting elements. The goal was not to fill space. It was to preserve attention.

Platform Consistency and Accessibility

Familiar behaviors adapted for spatial input

Users still rely on platform conventions, even in a new interaction model. I aligned targets, spacing, and interaction zones with OS expectations while adapting them for eye tracking and gesture input.

Semantic state rules across layered surfaces
State Management in Depth

Visual states that remain stable across depth

Layered translucency can amplify contrast, blur, and opacity in unintended ways. I defined state behavior semantically so selection, hover, and emphasis remain consistent regardless of overlap or surface level.

System decision

Prevent state multiplication by separating semantic meaning from surface rendering.

Flexible Windowing

Freedom without fragmentation

I designed a windowing model where primary content remains anchored to main contexts while supporting surfaces can detach and reposition when needed. Movement only adds value when it preserves orientation and task continuity.

Unified Spatial System

Consistent across scenarios

Chat, meetings, calendar, and collaboration surfaces all share the same interaction language for hierarchy, movement, positioning, and focus.

System Principles

Principles that guided the work

Clarity over novelty

Use spatial behavior to reduce ambiguity, not to create spectacle.

Depth as hierarchy

Depth should communicate role and focus, not decoration.

Cross platform continuity

Keep the experience recognizably Teams across devices and inputs.

Accessibility as structure

Define accessibility constraints at the system level from the start.

Flexibility with orientation

Support movement and multitasking without losing context.

Outcome

A framework that can scale beyond a single launch

This work shipped as part of the first Microsoft Teams experience on Apple Vision Pro. More importantly, it established a spatial framework that supports future product expansion. The layer model, windowing logic, accessibility guidance, and interaction patterns turned a new platform challenge into a scalable system.

Reflection

The most valuable outcome was the system itself

New platforms require clear principles early. Without them, spatial UI quickly becomes fragmented. This work reinforced that design systems are not only useful for scale across teams and screens. They are equally critical when extending products into entirely new interaction models.
